32 Which component has the I–V graph shown?
I
V
0
0
A
filament lamp
B
metallic conductor at constant temperature
C
resistor of fixed resistance
D
semiconductor diode

hints: Look at the shape of the $I$ against $V$ curve from the origin - it starts steep then bends over so its gradient gets smaller as $V$ gets larger.
Remember that gradient of an $I$-$V$ graph equals $1/R$, so a decreasing gradient means the resistance $R = V/I$ is increasing with current.
Ask which listed component heats up significantly as current flows so that increased lattice vibration raises its resistance.
walkthrough: Identify the axes: current $I$ is plotted vertically against potential difference $V$ horizontally, starting at $0,0$.
Check the gradient: the curve is steep at small $V$ then flattens, so $\Delta I / \Delta V$ decreases as $V$ and $I$ increase.
Use the rule that for an $I$-$V$ graph, gradient $= 1/R$, so decreasing gradient means resistance $R = V/I$ is increasing.
Link to heating effect: larger $I$ dissipates power $P = IV$ in the component, raising its temperature and increasing resistance due to more ion vibration scattering electrons.
Contrast with the other options: constant-resistance conductors give a straight line, while a diode stays near $I=0$ then rises very sharply.
The gradual flattening due to temperature rise is characteristic of a filament lamp. This is option A.

A.explanation: The curve flattens as $V$ increases, showing resistance increasing with temperature, which matches a heating filament.

B.explanation: An ohmic metallic conductor at constant temperature obeys $I = V/R$ and would give a straight line through the origin.

C.explanation: A resistor of fixed resistance is ohmic, so its $I$-$V$ graph is a straight line with constant gradient $1/R$.

D.explanation: A diode conducts sharply in one direction only, giving near-zero $I$ then a very steep rise, not a gradual flattening curve.
